prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Whoever, Fire, Not

outputs.L1:
Whoever it was who brought that first wood and coal
To kindle the Fire performed his part well;
For not all wood will take to flame from a match,
Nor coal from wood until it burns to charcoal.
The wood and coal in question caught a flame
And flared up beautifully, reaching out to the air
That draws a flame from anything it touches.
Somehow the fire was gathered in its furnace,
And then the moment came for some to say,
"The proper banking of the furnace saves the coal."
I have watched them set to work, each in his own way,
Yet all alike with shovels and with ashes,
Never resting until the fire seemed all but dead;
Whereupon they would creep, in hooded night-caps,
Contentedly to bed. At times the fire, thus left alone,
Would perish; yet as often the smoldering embers,
Enduring by the hardest until day, would flicker up—
Never strong—for anyone who cared to rake for them.
But roaring fires have never been made in such a way.
I should like to tell those folk that one grand blaze,
Transferred to the enduring memory of the air,
Is worth as much—or, to dull minds that trade in gold,
More than all the money ever saved by banking coal.
outputs.L2:
The person responsible for hauling in that initial batch of wood and coal to get the Fire going performed the task admirably. After all, not every piece of wood will ignite from a simple match, and coal won't catch from burning wood until that wood has been reduced to charcoal first. But in this instance, both the wood and coal did ignite, blazing up magnificently as they met the air—air that will accept a flame from any source. Through some process the fire became contained within the furnace, and eventually the moment arrived when certain people would remark, "Properly banking the furnace conserves the coal."

I've watched these people go about their business, each following his own method, yet all of them wielding shovels and heaping on ashes. They wouldn't stop until the fire appeared nearly extinguished. Only then would they shuffle off, wearing their hooded night-caps, and climb happily into bed. On occasion, a fire left to itself would simply go out. But just as frequently, a few stubborn embers—clinging to life with great difficulty until morning—would still glow faintly for anyone willing to stir them up. These flames, however, were never robust.

Yet blazing, roaring fires have never been produced through such caution. I'd like to say to those cautious folks that a single splendid burst of flame, its heat imprinted upon the very memory of the air, holds as much value as—or, for the small-minded who measure worth in gold, more value than—all the money ever conserved by banking coal.
outputs.L3:
# On Building and Keeping Fires

The person who initially built the fire performed their task skillfully, for not all materials readily catch flame from a simple match or spark. Kindling a fire is an art in itself, requiring both knowledge and patience to coax the first tentative flames into life.

Once the wood and coal ignited, the fire flared beautifully and became well-established in its furnace. What began as a fragile flicker grew into something warm and enduring, radiating heat and light throughout the space it served.

Yet not everyone approaches the tending of a fire with the same philosophy. Some people focus their energy on "banking the furnace" to conserve coal, working diligently with their shovels and ashes until the fire nearly dies out. Only then, satisfied that they have saved every possible lump of fuel, do they go contentedly to bed.

But such caution carries its own risks. A carefully banked fire may sometimes die completely during the night, or at best produce only weak, flickering embers—faint glimmers that appear solely for those willing to rake through the ashes to find them. The reward for such thrift is often little more than cold comfort.

The truth is that great, roaring fires are never created through such cautious conservation. There is a lesson here that extends well beyond the furnace: one magnificent blaze, preserved forever in memory, is worth more than all the money one might save by carefully banking coal. It is better to burn brightly and generously than to hoard our resources so timidly that we never truly feel their warmth at all.
outputs.L4:
# On Fire and Living

The poem takes as its central image the building and tending of a fire, and from this simple domestic act it draws a rich meditation on how we choose to live our lives. Fire, after all, is both light and warmth, both spectacle and sustenance—and the way a person handles a flame reveals much about the way that person handles the gift of being alive.

At the heart of the poem lies a contrast between two kinds of people, embodied in two ways of tending a fire. On one side stand those who eagerly strike the match and build a bold, roaring blaze. They pile on the fuel without hesitation, delighting in the heat and brilliance of the moment, unafraid to let the flames leap high even if it means the wood will soon be gone. On the other side stand the cautious ones, who carefully "bank" their coals—pressing them down, covering them with ash, feeding the fire only sparingly so that it will smolder on and on. Their instinct is preservation. They measure every log, calculate every ember, and guard their fuel against a colder day that may or may not ever come.

Through this extended metaphor, the poem asks a searching question: what is our energy for? Is it a resource to be hoarded, stretched thin across a long and careful lifetime, or is it something to be spent freely, even recklessly, in pursuit of intensity and joy? The banked fire represents a life lived defensively—a life of timid self-protection, in which one never risks too much for fear of running out. The bold blaze represents a life lived at full brightness, generous with itself, willing to burn hard even at the cost of burning out.

In its conclusion, the poem comes down firmly on the side of the flame. It argues that a single magnificent flare of passion—one moment of brilliant, unguarded life—is worth more than all the fuel a cautious soul might save. For such a moment does not truly vanish. It is preserved in memory, glowing there long after the fire itself has died, warming us in recollection as the hoarded coals never could. The careful person may end with resources intact, but with nothing bright to remember; the bold person may spend everything, yet carries forever the light of having truly lived.

Thus the poem becomes a quiet manifesto for bold living over careful preservation. It champions courage over caution, passion over prudence, and the willingness to be consumed by one's own fire over the safer instinct to smother it. Better, the poem insists, to blaze once and be remembered than to smolder long and be forgotten.
outputs.L5:
# Whoever Plays with Fire

There is an old saying that whoever plays with fire will eventually get burned. It is a warning passed down through generations, spoken by cautious parents and weary elders alike. Yet it is a lesson that many refuse to learn until the flames have already touched their skin.

Fire is neither good nor evil on its own. It is a tool, a force, a presence that can warm a home or destroy an entire forest. Whoever respects it may cook their meals, light their nights, and survive the coldest winters. But whoever ignores its danger does so at their own peril.

The problem is not the fire itself. The problem is carelessness. Whoever handles it without thought, without caution, without wisdom, invites disaster into their life. A single spark, left unattended, can grow into something that cannot be controlled or stopped.

So the message is clear, and it is not complicated. Whoever chooses to work with fire must also choose responsibility. Do not underestimate its power. Do not assume you are safe simply because nothing has gone wrong yet. And do not forget that respect, not fear, is what keeps the flame from becoming a threat.

In the end, whoever masters this balance will find that fire is a faithful servant. But whoever does not will learn the hardest lesson of all.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of Robert Frost about building and tending a fire, using the fire as a metaphor for passion versus caution in life.
counterfactuals.output:
**Tending the Fire**

I laid the kindling careful in the grate,
The way my father showed me, small to large,
And knew the flame would neither rush nor wait
But answer to the tending I could charge.

A fire wants for air, but not too much—
Too free a draft, and all your wood is spent
In one bright hour that burns beyond your touch,
And leaves you cold with nothing to prevent.

Yet bank it down too careful, too controlled,
And smother what you meant to keep alive;
The prudent hearth grows sullen, grey, and old,
And warmth withheld is warmth that won't survive.

I've known both men: the one who burned too fast,
Who gave his whole heart's cordwood to a day,
And one who saved his embers to the last
And died with all his kindling stowed away.

So here I kneel between the flame and frost
And weigh the coal against the open sky,
For every fire tended has its cost,
And every fire hoarded has to die.

I add a log. I crack the damper wide
Enough to let it breathe, but not to roar.
The trick, I've learned, is standing at the side
And knowing when to give it something more.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem about someone who starts a fire with wood and coal, and how some people "bank" the fire to save fuel while others let it blaze—make it a meditation on living boldly.
counterfactuals.output:
# On Tending Fire

She kneels at the cold mouth of morning,
arranging kindling like small prayers,
the wood still smelling of the forest it forgot,
and coal—black jewels of buried time,
sunlight pressed to stone
across ten thousand patient years.

The match. A hiss. That first
orange animal wakes and stretches,
licking the edges of the wood,
finding the seams, the splinters,
the places where fire remembers
how to be fire.

Now comes the choosing.

Some hands, careful hands,
will bank it—
mound the ash like a blanket,
smother the flame down to a sullen glow,
save the coal for the long dark,
keep the ember sleeping
so tomorrow will not find them empty.
This is wisdom, they say.
This is how you last.

And they are not wrong.
There is a season for the covered coal,
for the flame kept small enough
to carry through the night.

But she has watched too many
guard their heat so fiercely
they forgot the reason for the fire.
Have seen the careful ones grow cold
inside their own economy,
hoarding warmth against a winter
that arrives regardless,
finding at the end
a full woodpile
and a life unlived.

So she opens the damper wide.
Feeds the flame another log,
another, lets it climb and roar
and throw its wild light
against the walls,
lets the room go golden,
lets the heat spill out the open door
and into the indifferent street.

Let it blaze.

Because the coal was always going to burn.
Because the wood was always going to end.
Because the only question fire ever asks
is not *how long*
but *how bright*—

and she has made her answer,
kneeling in the dawn,
a small arsonist of joy,
setting her one life
gloriously,
irretrievably
alight.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a metaphorical poem comparing a roaring fire to bold self-expression, contrasting it with people who conserve and dampen their flames to save resources.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Ember and the Blaze

Some tend their fires with careful hands,
a measured breath, a rationed spark,
they bank the coals in prudent bands
and hoard their warmth against the dark.

*Not yet,* they say, *not here, not now—
the wood is scarce, the winter long.*
They dim the light behind the brow
and swallow back the rising song.

But I have watched a wildfire speak,
a throat of gold thrown open wide,
that does not ask permission, meek,
to let its brightness burn outside.

It crackles loud, it throws its sparks,
it climbs the air in reckless red,
it writes its name across the dark
and lives full-blazing till it's dead.

Yes—flame consumes. The careful know.
To burn is not to be preserved.
The tempered coal will slower glow,
its longer life more safely served.

And yet what good is stockpiled heat
that never dares to warm a room?
What treasure in a fire discreet
that guards its light straight to the tomb?

So let them save. Let embers keep.
I'll take the roar, the risk, the shine—
and if I burn, at least I'll leap
in language wholly, fiercely mine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a Frost-like blank verse poem about tending a furnace, where banking the coal represents timid, penny-pinching living, and one grand flare of fire is worth more than all savings.
counterfactuals.output:
**Banking the Fire**

I go down cellar when the night turns cold
And find the furnace waiting like a debt.
The trick, they told me, is to bank the coal—
To smother down the fire beneath its ash
So nothing burns too bright and nothing's lost,
And morning finds a coax of embers left
To build again from almost-nothing back.
I've done it forty winters, shy of flame,
And measured out my heat as men count coin,
Afraid to warm the house beyond its worth.

There is a kind of thrift that starves the room.
You keep the fire so careful and so low
It never roars, but neither does it die,
And you go up to bed a little chilled,
And call it wisdom, saving what you saved.
I've watched a whole life dampered down that way,
The draft pulled shut against the reckless dark,
Each glowing thing half-buried in its gray,
As if the sin were burning, not the cold.

But once, one bitter night, I let it go.
I threw the whole scuttle in and left it wide.
The grate took hold and shuddered into gold,
And such a light came climbing up the stair
The frosted windows ran with sudden thaw.
The house stood warm as summer for an hour.
It burned through all my banking in a night.

And I have thought since then it was worth more,
That one plain hour of unaccounted fire,
Than all the careful mornings I'd have bought
By hoarding embers I was scared to spend.
The coal will go to ash come either way.
Better it go to light. I bank no more.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about fire, charcoal, and coal that turns into a philosophical argument that a single memorable blaze matters more than a lifetime of caution.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Argument of Embers

Consider first the charcoal, black and mute,
a thing already burned, already spent,
that holds its heat in disciplined pursuit
of usefulness—reliable, content
to smolder low beneath a careful grate,
to never flare, to never overreach,
to warm the hands of those who calculate
the cost of every flame they might beseech.

And coal, entombed a hundred million years,
compressed by patience into stubborn stone—
what did it earn by hoarding all those tears
of ancient forests fallen and alone?
It waited, dense and dark and unafraid
of nothing, for it never risked a spark.
A lifetime is a fortune slowly made
and slowly kept, and buried in the dark.

But fire—fire does not negotiate.
It answers only to the wind and now.
It asks no permanence, it will not wait,
it makes no contract, offers you no vow
except this one: *I will consume myself
completely, and I will not ask you why.*
The candle does not measure out its wealth—
it spends the whole of what it is, to die.

So here's the argument the embers make
to every hoarded, unspent, cautious hour:
a single blaze the watching world can't shake
outweighs a vault of undischarged power.
Ten thousand nights of smoldering restraint
will not outshine one instant burning white—
the world remembers neither smoke nor saint,
but that one field that briefly *was* the light.

For what is caution but a slow decay,
a coal that dies still dreaming of the flame?
Better to burn the whole of you away
and leave behind one unforgotten name.
The charcoal keeps. The fire is what's *true*.
Choose, then, before your final ember dims:
a hundred years of almost-warming few—
or one bright roar they'll tell as after-hymns.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
